answer: The principal cardiovascular derangement is tachycardia, documented at all tested doses in dogs and the primary indication for beta-blocker therapy (e.g., esmolol) in albuterol toxicosis. Transient hypokalemia also occurs. At supratherapeutic doses, albuterol loses beta-2 selectivity and stimulates beta-1 adrenergic receptors as well, amplifying cardiovascular stimulation. In overdose, the duration of pharmacologic effects can extend up to 3 days.
explanation:
Albuterol is a synthetic sympathomimetic amine with primarily beta-2 adrenergic receptor agonist properties at therapeutic doses; with overdose, it exerts agonist effects on beta-1 adrenergic receptors as well. In a species-comparison toxicology study, dogs exposed to inhaled albuterol developed tachycardia and transient hypokalemia at all doses tested, with cardiovascular effects consistent with known beta-2 agonist pharmacology. A retrospective veterinary case series confirmed that albuterol ingestion in dogs produces tachycardia severe enough to warrant beta-blocker therapy (esmolol), with a 46% success rate for achieving at least a 20% heart-rate reduction. The pharmacokinetic profile notes rapid absorption and that in overdose, effects can persist up to 3 days, necessitating prolonged cardiovascular monitoring.
